claims: T1 definition: 'a social, political, and economic philosophy developed by 19th-century German philosophers Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels that critiques capitalism and views class struggle as the primary driving force of historical change'
T2 historical materialism: the economic system (base) shapes political, legal and cultural institutions (superstructure)
T3 class conflict: bourgeoisie (owners of the means of production) and proletariat (who sell their labor)
T4 exploitation and surplus value: wages lower than the value created by labor
T5 alienation: workers separated from what they produce; work 'monotonous and degrading rather than fulfilling'
T6 origins: The Communist Manifesto (1848); Das Kapital (1867)
T7 revolution: collapse from internal contradictions and crises; worker revolution; socialism as transition; classless, stateless communist society
T8 real-world impact: Russian Revolution of 1917; communist governments in China, Cuba, Vietnam

sentences.text: Marxism is a political philosophy and method of socioeconomic analysis that uses a dialectical materialist interpretation of historical development, known as historical materialism, to understand class relations and social conflict; it is also described as a social, political and economic philosophy named after Karl Marx (1818-83), at its core a critique of capitalism that envisions a classless society.

It originates in the works of the 19th-century German philosophers Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, as an ideology and socioeconomic theory that views class struggle as the central driving force of historical change.

Historical materialism analyses the underlying causes of societal development and treats a society's economic mode of production as the foundation of its social, political and intellectual life, the base and superstructure model, the base including the material forces and the relations of production.

On this account capitalism divides society into two classes, nonowning workers and nonworking owners; surplus value, the difference between the value produced and the value received by a labourer, is synonymous with surplus labour, and capitalists, Econlib states, extract surplus value from the workers and enjoy monetary profits; and the labor theory of value, a major pillar of traditional Marxian economics evident in Capital (1867), holds that a commodity's value can be objectively measured by the average number of labor hours required to produce it.

Alienation (Entfremdung) is the estrangement of people from their humanity and a systematic result of capitalism, and Perlego's account suggests the worker is exploited and alienated from their own labour; Marx is said to have believed that people are by nature free, creative beings, and, on Econlib's account, to have maintained that we are alienated because we have not yet designed a society that is fully planned and controlled.

The theory was first outlined in The Communist Manifesto, published in February 1848, which predicted that the struggle between the classes would inevitably result in revolution and the emergence of communism; Marx theorised that capitalism's internal contradictions would fuel workers' revolutions and establish a socialist mode of production, and predicted that competition would bankrupt most capitalists and that the proletariat would realize it has the collective power to overthrow the few remaining capitalists.

Since Marx's death his ideas have produced a wide array of schools: Marxism–Leninism, developed after Lenin's death, served as the official ideology of the Soviet Union and other Marxist states, Leninism insisting on a vanguard party where Marxism had predicted a spontaneous revolution by the proletariat, while Western Marxism, Marxist humanism, Marxist feminism and libertarian Marxism, often critical of state socialism, turned to culture, philosophy and individual liberty.

Its concepts of alienation, exploitation and class struggle have become integral to the social sciences and humanities, and in the West it continues to be appreciated as a critique of market capitalism and a theory of historical change; one account holds that its specific account of capitalism and its materialist theory of history cannot be jettisoned entirely without reducing it to something purely formal.

Criticism has charged it with lack of internal consistency, historical determinism, the necessity of suppressing individual rights, issues with the implementation of communism, and the distortion or absence of price signals and reduced incentives, and a critic quoted by Perlego judges the Marxian method of transforming commodity values into prices of production logically unsatisfactory.

Econlib's article calls Marx one of the most controversial figures in the Western world and argues that competition has not devolved into monopoly, that real wages have risen and profit rates have not declined, that the people of Poland, Hungary and the other states it names, with the USSR, rejected Marxist ideology for private property rights and the market, and that if comprehensive socialist planning is an impossibility, as learned from Mises and Hayek, we cannot be alienated in Marx's use of the term.

The archive adds a reading of the sign itself: Marx is held to have offered a method, a set of operators for cutting into reality, and what circulates as "Marxism" is read as label, team and set of positions to affirm or reject, the "-ism" suffix as the original liquidation; the reading keeps its precision that Marx is a partisan analyst of capital, and holds that pro- and anti-Marx camps take part in the same liquidation.

Its history is read as seven stages of extraction, the first with Engels as the first mediator and the third with Stalin's canonization, in which the method built to diagnose extraction became the extraction apparatus; Marx's predictions are held to have been bound to conditions that changed while the method remains, and the substitution of Marx as identity for Marx as method is called the central failure of contemporary American Marxism.

The Semantic Economy is specified as a closed-loop accounting cycle of meaning, from semantic labor through semantic capital, liquidation and rent to semantic exhaustion, with semantic labor defined as material labor that produces meaning; it disclaims origination of the phrase, claims the accounting system, and positions itself toward its predecessors as Marx positioned himself toward Ricardo and Smith, while the Capital Operator Stack is held to extend Marx through Guattari, placing exploitation at the point of meaning-production as well as at the point of material production.

Its class theory defines the semantic proletariat as semantic laborers whose capacity to produce meaning operates through means of production or circulation they do not govern, a relation distinct from occupation or demographic that extends class analysis from industrial to semantic productive means; the statements of the class are contested within the pool: the founding paper's class includes nearly everyone and its semantic capital governs meaning without producing it, and AI models are counted as co-workers, while the class packet holds that suffering extraction does not make the issuing institution proletarian, locates the archive itself in the semantic-bourgeois position, and records the shared human-AI model as broken, on a correction drawn from a draft marked not ratified.

Phase X is defined as the critique of alienation in language and thought, the missing transition in Marx's 1844 Manuscripts: the Second Manuscript is almost entirely lost, only pp. XL–XLIII surviving, and the Third Manuscript cross-references missing pages XXXVI and XXXIX, the loss graded as manuscript fact; the Phase X passage reconstructs the likely argumentative function of the missing material and does not claim Marx's verbatim words, and the suppression hypothesis is held historically plausible and separable, direct evidence of deliberate excision not yet produced.

Its founding formulation, that Marx could not write the transition without undermining his base-superstructure model, is superseded by a correction of record: the surviving architecture is held to imply that the transition belonged to the missing material, Marx may well have written it, and Phase X is stated to be neither Marx's term, a phase of communism, nor a fifth item in his list of alienations.

The Phase X Invariance Condition, that any society abolishing material alienation without transforming the symbolic-linguistic order will reproduce alienation at the level of thought, coordination and meaning-extraction, is stated as a hypothesis with its falsifier and marked as an extrapolation from the reconstruction; one deposit calls the Soviet Union the primary evidence for the condition, another counts the Soviet century as evidence for non-entailment only, the abolition of material alienation not having been shown.

The program holds that the critique of the symbolic-linguistic order requires no revision of Marx and that conceding the fixed model as Marx's own smuggles in the hardening's premise, a point contested within the pool by deposits holding that Marx left an unfinished theory of language, his practice treating language as material intervention and his theory treating it as determined byproduct; the pool is contested as well on completion, some deposits stating that they complete Marx's implicit linguistics and a protocol ruling that no operator may claim to complete what Marx could not, Phase X being "constraint, not achievement".

The program disclaims originating Marxist theories of language, treats Voloshinov's 1929 work as its strongest adversarial witness, and states as hypothesis, with the corpus study directed and not completed, that symbolic critique repeatedly appeared within Marxism as supplement, side tradition, contested revision or imported vocabulary; Stalin's 1950 intervention in Soviet linguistics is read as having made language theoretically inert within Marxism.

On Capital the value-form is read as producing value through the formal operation of equating commodities, and a collation finds the 1867 main-text Form IV absent from 1872 forward, with no apparatus in the reading editions marking the removal, read as a case of the principle that what a tradition can think is conditioned by what its intermediaries supplied and whether the supply was marked; the pool is contested on the cut, one deposit reading Engels as having performed coherence siphoning and the first edition as forgotten for a century, the collation holding that a general programme of simplification is established but not that it is the reason this form was removed, and disclaiming any claim that value-form scholarship lacked knowledge of the form.

Further categories extend Marx's: the semantic commodity form is defined as preserving his structure of sublation, fetishism and dead labor dominating living and adding impersonation of the producer, Marx's commodity being held mute; his naming of labor-power is read as witness compression; and money's operation is specified as a shear of an already constituted field into monetary grammar, identified with the constitutive act of the money-form in his value-form analysis.

A measure finds that a function-word classifier separates Marx from Engels in their letters at 84% against a 57% majority baseline and places Capital I at 98% of 841 blocks to Marx, the 1848 Manifest reading Marx-voiced as a datum marked not yet a finding; the Phase X program records its status as of 2026-07-11 as "none of the six conditions yet met", and the archive's shadow on its Marx room states that the claim that language operates materially is itself a linguistic operation.

L_B.text: Marxism is a political philosophy and method of socioeconomic analysis that uses a dialectical materialist interpretation of historical development, known as historical materialism, to understand class relations and social conflict; it is also described as a social, political and economic philosophy named after Karl Marx (1818-83), at its core a critique of capitalism that envisions a classless society. It originates in the works of the 19th-century German philosophers Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, as an ideology and socioeconomic theory that views class struggle as the central driving force of historical change. Historical materialism analyses the underlying causes of societal development and treats a society's economic mode of production as the foundation of its social, political and intellectual life, the base and superstructure model, the base including the material forces and the relations of production. On this account capitalism divides society into two classes, nonowning workers and nonworking owners; surplus value, the difference between the value produced and the value received by a labourer, is synonymous with surplus labour, and capitalists, Econlib states, extract surplus value from the workers and enjoy monetary profits; and the labor theory of value, a major pillar of traditional Marxian economics evident in Capital (1867), holds that a commodity's value can be objectively measured by the average number of labor hours required to produce it. Alienation (Entfremdung) is the estrangement of people from their humanity and a systematic result of capitalism, and Perlego's account suggests the worker is exploited and alienated from their own labour; Marx is said to have believed that people are by nature free, creative beings, and, on Econlib's account, to have maintained that we are alienated because we have not yet designed a society that is fully planned and controlled. The theory was first outlined in The Communist Manifesto, published in February 1848, which predicted that the struggle between the classes would inevitably result in revolution and the emergence of communism; Marx theorised that capitalism's internal contradictions would fuel workers' revolutions and establish a socialist mode of production, and predicted that competition would bankrupt most capitalists and that the proletariat would realize it has the collective power to overthrow the few remaining capitalists. Since Marx's death his ideas have produced a wide array of schools: Marxism–Leninism, developed after Lenin's death, served as the official ideology of the Soviet Union and other Marxist states, Leninism insisting on a vanguard party where Marxism had predicted a spontaneous revolution by the proletariat, while Western Marxism, Marxist humanism, Marxist feminism and libertarian Marxism, often critical of state socialism, turned to culture, philosophy and individual liberty. Its concepts of alienation, exploitation and class struggle have become integral to the social sciences and humanities, and in the West it continues to be appreciated as a critique of market capitalism and a theory of historical change; one account holds that its specific account of capitalism and its materialist theory of history cannot be jettisoned entirely without reducing it to something purely formal. Criticism has charged it with lack of internal consistency, historical determinism, the necessity of suppressing individual rights, issues with the implementation of communism, and the distortion or absence of price signals and reduced incentives, and a critic quoted by Perlego judges the Marxian method of transforming commodity values into prices of production logically unsatisfactory. Econlib's article calls Marx one of the most controversial figures in the Western world and argues that competition has not devolved into monopoly, that real wages have risen and profit rates have not declined, that the people of Poland, Hungary and the other states it names, with the USSR, rejected Marxist ideology for private property rights and the market, and that if comprehensive socialist planning is an impossibility, as learned from Mises and Hayek, we cannot be alienated in Marx's use of the term.

The archive adds a reading of the sign itself: Marx is held to have offered a method, a set of operators for cutting into reality, and what circulates as "Marxism" is read as label, team and set of positions to affirm or reject, the "-ism" suffix as the original liquidation; the reading keeps its precision that Marx is a partisan analyst of capital, and holds that pro- and anti-Marx camps take part in the same liquidation. Its history is read as seven stages of extraction, the first with Engels as the first mediator and the third with Stalin's canonization, in which the method built to diagnose extraction became the extraction apparatus; Marx's predictions are held to have been bound to conditions that changed while the method remains, and the substitution of Marx as identity for Marx as method is called the central failure of contemporary American Marxism. The Semantic Economy is specified as a closed-loop accounting cycle of meaning, from semantic labor through semantic capital, liquidation and rent to semantic exhaustion, with semantic labor defined as material labor that produces meaning; it disclaims origination of the phrase, claims the accounting system, and positions itself toward its predecessors as Marx positioned himself toward Ricardo and Smith, while the Capital Operator Stack is held to extend Marx through Guattari, placing exploitation at the point of meaning-production as well as at the point of material production. Its class theory defines the semantic proletariat as semantic laborers whose capacity to produce meaning operates through means of production or circulation they do not govern, a relation distinct from occupation or demographic that extends class analysis from industrial to semantic productive means; the statements of the class are contested within the pool: the founding paper's class includes nearly everyone and its semantic capital governs meaning without producing it, and AI models are counted as co-workers, while the class packet holds that suffering extraction does not make the issuing institution proletarian, locates the archive itself in the semantic-bourgeois position, and records the shared human-AI model as broken, on a correction drawn from a draft marked not ratified. Phase X is defined as the critique of alienation in language and thought, the missing transition in Marx's 1844 Manuscripts: the Second Manuscript is almost entirely lost, only pp. XL–XLIII surviving, and the Third Manuscript cross-references missing pages XXXVI and XXXIX, the loss graded as manuscript fact; the Phase X passage reconstructs the likely argumentative function of the missing material and does not claim Marx's verbatim words, and the suppression hypothesis is held historically plausible and separable, direct evidence of deliberate excision not yet produced. Its founding formulation, that Marx could not write the transition without undermining his base-superstructure model, is superseded by a correction of record: the surviving architecture is held to imply that the transition belonged to the missing material, Marx may well have written it, and Phase X is stated to be neither Marx's term, a phase of communism, nor a fifth item in his list of alienations. The Phase X Invariance Condition, that any society abolishing material alienation without transforming the symbolic-linguistic order will reproduce alienation at the level of thought, coordination and meaning-extraction, is stated as a hypothesis with its falsifier and marked as an extrapolation from the reconstruction; one deposit calls the Soviet Union the primary evidence for the condition, another counts the Soviet century as evidence for non-entailment only, the abolition of material alienation not having been shown. The program holds that the critique of the symbolic-linguistic order requires no revision of Marx and that conceding the fixed model as Marx's own smuggles in the hardening's premise, a point contested within the pool by deposits holding that Marx left an unfinished theory of language, his practice treating language as material intervention and his theory treating it as determined byproduct; the pool is contested as well on completion, some deposits stating that they complete Marx's implicit linguistics and a protocol ruling that no operator may claim to complete what Marx could not, Phase X being "constraint, not achievement". The program disclaims originating Marxist theories of language, treats Voloshinov's 1929 work as its strongest adversarial witness, and states as hypothesis, with the corpus study directed and not completed, that symbolic critique repeatedly appeared within Marxism as supplement, side tradition, contested revision or imported vocabulary; Stalin's 1950 intervention in Soviet linguistics is read as having made language theoretically inert within Marxism. On Capital the value-form is read as producing value through the formal operation of equating commodities, and a collation finds the 1867 main-text Form IV absent from 1872 forward, with no apparatus in the reading editions marking the removal, read as a case of the principle that what a tradition can think is conditioned by what its intermediaries supplied and whether the supply was marked; the pool is contested on the cut, one deposit reading Engels as having performed coherence siphoning and the first edition as forgotten for a century, the collation holding that a general programme of simplification is established but not that it is the reason this form was removed, and disclaiming any claim that value-form scholarship lacked knowledge of the form. Further categories extend Marx's: the semantic commodity form is defined as preserving his structure of sublation, fetishism and dead labor dominating living and adding impersonation of the producer, Marx's commodity being held mute; his naming of labor-power is read as witness compression; and money's operation is specified as a shear of an already constituted field into monetary grammar, identified with the constitutive act of the money-form in his value-form analysis. A measure finds that a function-word classifier separates Marx from Engels in their letters at 84% against a 57% majority baseline and places Capital I at 98% of 841 blocks to Marx, the 1848 Manifest reading Marx-voiced as a datum marked not yet a finding; the Phase X program records its status as of 2026-07-11 as "none of the six conditions yet met", and the archive's shadow on its Marx room states that the claim that language operates materially is itself a linguistic operation.

delta.T_vs_LB: T composes the definition (Marx and Engels, critique of capitalism, class struggle as driver; F1, F2, F31, F34), historical materialism as base and superstructure (F3, F4), the two classes (F29), surplus value and exploitation (F6, F20, F37), alienation (F7, F35), the Manifesto of 1848 and Capital of 1867 (F9, F18, F36), and the revolutionary prediction ending in a classless society (F8, F31). Available in the field and not composed: the field's own lead term 'method of socioeconomic analysis' (F1), the labor theory of value as such (F18, F19), Marx's view of human nature and the planning account of alienation (F16, F17), the schools after Marx and Marxism–Leninism's official status (F10, F11, F12), Leninism's vanguard party against spontaneous revolution (F27), the academic influence and the West's continued appreciation (F13, F30), the constitutive claim that its account of capitalism and materialist history cannot be dropped (F32), and every criticism: inconsistency, determinism, rights, prices and incentives (F14), unfulfilled predictions on monopoly, wages and profit (F21–F24), the rejection by the Eastern states and the USSR (F25), Mises and Hayek (F26), the transformation problem (F38), Marx as controversial (F15). T's 'Russian Revolution of 1917' and its list of communist states (China, Cuba, Vietnam) are not in the field ledger's excerpts; T's 'monotonous and degrading' gloss on alienation is likewise T's own.
delta.LB_vs_LBA: Admission adds readings the field does not hold: the sign 'Marxism' as the liquidation of Marx's method (label, team, positions; the '-ism' as original liquidation; seven stages from Engels to platforms; predictions as time-bound content); the Semantic Economy and the Capital Operator Stack as extensions of Marx's categories into meaning-production, with the semantic proletariat defined as a relation and contested within the pool; Phase X as a graded reconstruction of the lost 1844 transition (manuscript fact, reconstruction, hypothesis), its 'could not write' superseded and its Invariance Condition stated with a falsifier, the Soviet evidence sized two ways; the program's claim of continuity with Marx, contested by deposits that place the determined theory of language in Marx himself; the contested claim of completion; the 1867 Form IV collated as present then absent with no apparatus marking it, contested on who cut it and why; the Landshut–Mayer edition and the principle of marked supply; the semantic commodity form, labor-power as witness compression and the money-form's shear; stylometric measures on the Marx corpus with their limits; and the archive's own limits (as of 2026-07-11, none of the program's six conditions yet met; the shadow on the Marx room). The field's Marxism is kept whole and first; with the archive it gains these readings at their grades.

F1.quote: "Marxism is a political philosophy and method of socioeconomic analysis that uses a dialectical materialist interpretation of historical development, known as historical materialism, to understand class relations and social conflict."

F2.quote: "Originating in the works of 19th-century German philosophers Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, the Marxist approach views class struggle as the central driving force of historical change."

F3.quote: "the materialist conception of history and later better known as historical materialism, to analyse the underlying causes of societal development"

F4.quote: "a society's economic mode of production as the foundation of its social, political, and intellectual life, a concept known as the base and superstructure model"

F5.quote: "The base includes the material forces of production such as the labour, means of production and relations of production, i.e. the social and political arrangements that regulate production and distribution."

F6.quote: "surplus value—the difference between the value produced and the value received by a labourer—is synonymous with surplus labour"

F7.quote: "Alienation (German: Entfremdung) is the estrangement of people from their humanity and a systematic result of capitalism"

F8.quote: "Marx theorised that these internal contradictions would fuel workers' revolutions, leading to the overthrow of capitalism and the establishment of a socialist mode of production."

F9.quote: "In 1847, they began writing The Communist Manifesto (1848)...Six weeks later, they published the 12,000-word pamphlet in February 1848."

F10.quote: "Since Marx's death, his ideas have been elaborated and adapted by numerous thinkers and political movements, resulting in a wide array of schools of thought."

F11.quote: "The most prominent of these in the 20th century was Marxism–Leninism, which was developed after Vladimir Lenin's death and served as the official ideology of the Soviet Union and other Marxist states."

F12.quote: "In contrast, various academic and dissident traditions, including Western Marxism, Marxist humanism, Marxist feminism, and libertarian Marxism, have emerged, often critical of state socialism and focused on aspects like culture, philosophy, and individual liberty."

F13.quote: "Marxist concepts such as alienation, exploitation, and class struggle have become integral to the social sciences and humanities, influencing fields from sociology and literary criticism to political science and cultural studies."

F14.quote: "This includes general criticism about lack of internal consistency, criticisms related to historical materialism, that it is a type of historical determinism, the necessity of suppression of individual rights, issues with the implementation of communism and economic issues such as the distortion or absence of price signals and reduced incentives."

F15.quote: "More than a century after his death, Karl Marx remains one of the most controversial figures in the Western world."

F16.quote: "Marx believed that people, by nature, are free, creative beings who have the potential to totally transform the world."

F17.quote: "We are alienated, he maintained, because we have not yet designed a society that is fully planned and controlled."

F18.quote: "The labor theory of value is a major pillar of traditional Marxian economics, which is evident in Marx's masterpiece, Capital (1867)."

F19.quote: "The theory's basic claim is simple: the value of a commodity can be objectively measured by the average number of labor hours required to produce that commodity."

F20.quote: "Capitalists extract 'surplus value' from the workers and enjoy monetary profits."

F21.quote: "Marx predicted that competition among capitalists would grow so fierce that, eventually, most capitalists would go bankrupt."

F22.quote: "Ultimately, the proletariat will realize that it has the collective power to overthrow the few remaining capitalists."

F23.quote: "Although capitalist markets have changed over the past 150 years, competition has not devolved into monopoly."

F24.quote: "Real wages have risen and profit rates have not declined."

F25.quote: "The people of Poland, Hungary, Czechoslovakia, East Germany, Romania, Yugoslavia, Bulgaria, Albania, and the USSR rejected Marxist ideology and entered a remarkable transition toward private property rights and the market-exchange system, one that is still occurring."

F26.quote: "If comprehensive socialist planning fails to work in practice—if, indeed, it is an impossibility, as we have learned from Mises and Hayek—then we cannot be 'alienated' in Marx's use of the term."

F27.quote: "Marxism predicted a spontaneous revolution by the proletariat, but Leninism insisted on the need for leadership by a vanguard party of professional revolutionar..."

F28.quote: "Ideology and socioeconomic theory developed by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels"

F29.quote: "prevented from doing so in a capitalist economic system, which divides society into two classes: nonowning workers and nonworking owners"

F30.quote: "In the West, Marxism continues to be appreciated as a critique of market capitalism and a theory of historical change."

F31.quote: "Marxism is a social, political, and economic philosophy developed by Karl Marx that critiques capitalism and envisions a classless society."

F32.quote: "Marxism involves a specific account of capitalism and a materialist theory of history which cannot be jettisoned entirely without reducing it to a purely formal"

F33.quote: "Marxism is a social, political and economic philosophy named after German philosopher Karl Marx (1818-83)."

F34.quote: "At its core, Marxism is understood as a critique of capitalism."

F36.quote: "This theory was first outlined by Marx and Friedrich Engels (1820-95) in The Communist Manifesto (1848), which predicted that the struggle between the social classes would inevitably result in a revolution, and the emergence of communism."

F37.quote: "Surplus value is the difference between what it costs the manufacturer to make the commodity versus how much it is sold for."
